title: My BTC bot beat plain DCA in the backtest. Live, it tied. The exits were the real problem.
author: Bright_Clerk1452

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: 'if a human overrides the bot you're grading the human' is the line most people never get to. and the exits result is the normal one: a DCA bot with a stop is two strategies, and the sell half gets judged against holding, which in BTC's case is a brutal benchmark. the buy signals were never where the money was.

replies.author: Bright_Clerk1452
replies.body:
yeah, splitting it into two strategies is the right way to see it. the buy side barely mattered: signal-weighted buying tied plain DCA within a fraction of a percent. all the damage came from the sell side, and you’re right that “vs just holding BTC” is about as unforgiving a benchmark as exists.

the human override part is what surprised me most. once someone sells by hand for their own reasons, the record stops measuring the strategy and starts measuring the person. which makes me think any honest track record has to log overrides as their own events, not blend them in.

curious if you’ve seen anyone handle that well, bots or signal groups that separate “what the system did” from “what the person did”?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the clean follow-up is running plain DCA and DCA-with-your-exits on the same window and reading only the gap, since the buy signal tied anyway. my guess from the numbers you posted is the stop did most of the damage on the deep dips, which is exactly where holding wins in BTC.

replies.author: Bright_Clerk1452
replies.body:
You called it. I ran exactly that: same buys, only the exits changed, 31 rolling 1-year windows.

The old exit set (regime TP/SL plus a trailing stop) came out a median 24 points behind plain DCA. Isolating the stop made it obvious. A -15% stop alone took the 3-year result from +13.0% to -10.7%, because it kept selling the deep dips that holding recovers from. At -25% it never fired in this sample, so the result just matched holding.

So v2 dropped the selling stop entirely (it's an alert now) and kept only a slow take-profit ladder, 25% off every +50%. That version beat plain DCA in 22 of 31 windows, by a median of about 1.7 points. Not huge, and the ladder itself added close to nothing. Most of the edge was sizing plus limit orders cutting fees.

I'm running it forward now with the rules locked so I can't tweak it mid-test. I'll post the result when the 30 days are up.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Honest write-up, and reporting every window instead of the best one is rare. On exits, I'd keep them as simple as possible with very few settings, then run them across many different start dates and compare each one with just holding. Look at the worst windows, not the median, and keep a stretch of data aside that you never touched while tuning. If I only saw the two year number, I'd ask for all windows and the fees on each sell. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is built for this kind of check, with out-of-sample data and fees included.

replies.author: Bright_Clerk1452
replies.body:
Thanks, all fair points. Two things I'd own up to.

There was no held-out stretch. Every variant was tuned and scored on the same three years, so the ladder's small edge could easily be overfit. And you're right about the worst windows. The median hides how bad the bad starts were, so I'll add a worst-window column and the fees on each sell to the next write-up.

My answer to the out-of-sample problem is to run it forward instead of carving up the past: rules locked before the first trade, no tweaks for 30 days, real fills and real fees. The past can always be fit, but next month can't. I'll post the result with every trade when the window ends.
